strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important limitation of autoregressive long video generation: inability to condition on future camera poses, which can cause collisions and rollout collapse under predefined trajectories.

The proposed Generative View Stitching formulation is conceptually appealing and practical: it is training-free, reuses off-the-shelf Diffusion Forcing video models, and adapts diffusion stitching to camera-guided video generation.
Omni Guidance and cyclic conditioning are well-motivated components, and the paper includes useful ablations showing their roles in temporal consistency, oversmoothing, and loop closure.

The experimental section compares against relevant baselines using the same backbone, includes multiple challenging camera trajectories, reports several metrics, and provides qualitative evidence for collision avoidance and loop consistency.

The paper is generally clear, with good illustrations and unusually candid discussion of limitations such as poor external image conditioning, wide-baseline failure cases, and dependence on the backbone model.
weaknesses: The evaluation is limited to a single Diffusion Forcing backbone trained on RealEstate10K, so the claim of broad compatibility with any DF video model is not empirically demonstrated.
Several benchmarks are synthetic or hand-designed camera trajectories, and it is unclear how representative they are of realistic camera-guided video generation use cases.

The loop-closing mechanism relies on manually specified spatial windows tailored to trajectory classes, which weakens the impression of a general-purpose method and may require nontrivial engineering for new paths.

The quantitative metrics are imperfect proxies for the central visual claims. MEt3R, VBench IQ/AQ, depth-threshold collision detection, and inception score may not fully capture temporal coherence, geometry, or user-perceived quality; no human evaluation is reported.

The method appears computationally expensive because it denoises many context windows over the entire sequence, but runtime, memory, and scaling comparisons against autoregressive sampling are only lightly discussed.

Some core claims depend strongly on qualitative videos, yet the manuscript text provides limited standalone evidence for video quality and failure frequency beyond selected frames and averaged metrics.

Novelty is meaningful but incremental: the work combines existing ideas from diffusion stitching, stochastic synchronization, classifier-free/inner guidance, and retrieval-like loop closure in a new video setting rather than introducing a fundamentally new model or training paradigm.

strengths: Addresses a relevant limitation of autoregressive long video generation: inability to condition current generation on future camera trajectory constraints.
The proposed method is simple and training-free for Diffusion Forcing video models, which is practically appealing if the assumptions hold.
The paper includes useful ablations for stochasticity, Omni Guidance, and loop-closing, and it is unusually candid about several failure modes in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the central claims. The benchmark is small, synthetic/hand-designed, and evaluated on a single backbone trained on RealEstate10K, making it hard to judge generality.

The main results depend heavily on visual/video quality, but the PDF only shows sparse frame strips and the project-page URL appears missing. This makes the most important claims difficult to verify from the submission.

The metrics are not fully convincing. MEt3R-based consistency, VBench quality, and inferred-depth collision detection are indirect proxies and may not capture scene stability, trajectory faithfulness, loop closure quality, or perceptual artifacts. No human study or stronger geometric validation is provided.

Baseline coverage and fairness are limited. StochSync is repurposed from a different setting, AR is evaluated with a particular memory augmentation, and there are no comparisons to broader long-video, view-synthesis, or trajectory-conditioned methods beyond this narrow setup.

Novelty is moderate rather than strong: the work mainly adapts diffusion stitching ideas to Diffusion Forcing models, with Omni Guidance and cyclic conditioning presented as useful heuristics but not deeply justified theoretically.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially claims of collision-free, stable, loop-closing generation across varied trajectories. The appendices show important failures with external context frames, wide-baseline loop closure, and ambiguous trajectories.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper reports hyperparameters and compute, but it is unclear whether code, trajectory benchmarks, generated videos, and evaluation scripts are released. The missing project link is a notable issue for a video-generation paper.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and meaningful contribution: Generative View Stitching, a training-free stitching method for camera-guided long video generation using existing Diffusion Forcing video models.

The motivation is compelling and well articulated: autoregressive sampling cannot condition on future camera trajectory constraints, leading to collisions and rollout collapse, while parallel stitching can incorporate future context.

The method is technically interesting, especially the observation that Diffusion Forcing models already provide the affordances needed for stitching without retraining, and the Omni Guidance mechanism is a plausible and useful adaptation of guidance to this setting.

The evaluation includes relevant baselines, including history-guided autoregressive sampling and StochSync, and uses the same backbone model across methods, which makes the comparison reasonably controlled.

The experiments show consistent gains on temporal consistency, long-range consistency, and collision avoidance across multiple challenging camera trajectories, with ablations supporting the roles of stochasticity, Omni Guidance, and explicit loop closing.
The qualitative results and application to an impossible staircase are memorable and well matched to the paper's claims, demonstrating capabilities that are difficult for autoregressive approaches.

The paper is unusually candid about limitations, including poor propagation of external image conditioning, failure on wide-baseline loop closure, and ambiguities from structurally similar camera paths.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies on a single Diffusion Forcing backbone trained on RealEstate10K, so the claim of compatibility with any off-the-shelf DF video model is not empirically tested across architectures, datasets, or model scales.
The benchmark trajectories appear to be author-designed rather than drawn from a standardized benchmark, making it harder to assess generality and compare future work fairly.

Several claims are primarily supported by qualitative evidence or proxy metrics. Metrics such as MEt3R consistency, VBench IQ/AQ, and inferred-depth collision detection are useful but imperfect proxies for human-perceived video coherence, physical plausibility, and camera-trajectory faithfulness.

The method introduces substantial test-time computation through parallel/chunked denoising and cyclic conditioning, but the paper provides limited quantitative runtime, memory, or cost comparisons against baselines.
Loop closure depends on hand-designed spatial context windows for each trajectory family, which may limit automation and general applicability to arbitrary paths.

The method's dependence on the backbone's camera-conditioning distribution is a significant limitation: the wide-baseline failure case suggests that GVS may not solve hard view-consistency problems beyond the support of the underlying model.

The derivation of Omni Guidance is intuitive but not fully rigorous; the practical merged guidance formula is heuristic, and the relationship between the proposed guided score and the intended conditional distribution could be better justified.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear limitation of autoregressive long video generation: inability to condition current generation on future camera poses, leading to collisions and collapse under predefined trajectories.

The proposed GVS sampler is technically sensible and practically attractive because it is training-free and leverages Diffusion Forcing-style per-frame noise conditioning rather than requiring a custom stitching-trained model.
Omni Guidance and cyclic conditioning are well-motivated components, with ablations showing their distinct roles in temporal consistency, stochasticity/oversmoothing tradeoffs, and loop closure.

The experiments compare against relevant baselines, including history-guided autoregressive sampling and StochSync, and include quantitative metrics, qualitative examples, runtime/memory analysis, and several appendix ablations across backbone variants and hyperparameters.

The paper is candid about important limitations, including offline-only applicability, weak external image conditioning, wide-baseline loop-closing failures, dependence on the backbone training distribution, and manually specified spatial windows.
weaknesses: The evaluation setting is narrow and largely constructed by the authors: a small set of predefined camera trajectories on a RealEstate10K-trained 8-frame backbone. It is unclear how well the method transfers to more diverse scenes, real cinematography workflows, or modern large-scale video diffusion systems.

Several key claims rely on proxy metrics such as MEt3R consistency and depth-threshold collision detection, plus selected qualitative strips. There is no human evaluation or task-level validation, which is a significant gap for generative video quality, temporal plausibility, and loop-closure realism.

The loop-closing mechanism depends on manually defined spatial windows per trajectory, limiting scalability and making part of the method trajectory-specific despite broader claims about camera-guided generation.

The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental: the core idea adapts diffusion stitching/composition to video generation, while the main technical additions are guidance and cyclic conditioning rather than a fundamentally new generative framework.

The claim of compatibility with any off-the-shelf Diffusion Forcing video model is plausible but not fully established; experiments use closely related backbones from the same source/training setup, and broader compatibility with current proprietary or large open video models is not demonstrated.
The method breaks causality and requires known future camera poses, so it does not address interactive or streaming generation, which are among the prominent use cases for long-horizon world models.

Some results reveal tradeoffs that are not fully resolved: stochasticity improves consistency partly by oversmoothing, loop closing can oversmooth, and wide-baseline viewpoints fail due to backbone distribution limits.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful and timely problem: long-horizon camera-guided video generation with predefined trajectories, where autoregressive rollout can fail because it cannot condition on future camera poses.
weaknesses: The empirical case is narrower than the claims. Most evidence is on hand-designed synthetic camera trajectories with one main public backbone, and the strongest results depend on trajectory-specific cyclic conditioning windows that are manually defined rather than generally inferred.

The evaluation relies heavily on proxy metrics such as MEt3R consistency, VBench IQ/AQ, and depth-threshold collision detection. For a video generation paper, the lack of a rigorous human study or stronger perceptual validation makes it hard to trust claims about visual consistency, oversmoothing, and loop closure quality.

Baselines are limited. The main comparisons are autoregressive history guidance and an adapted StochSync baseline; the paper does not convincingly compare to broader camera-controlled video generation, long-video generation, retrieval/memory-based methods, or planning-based collision avoidance systems under matched settings.

The proposed loop-closing mechanism weakens the generality of the contribution. Spatial windows are manually specified per trajectory, and the paper explicitly acknowledges this is not scalable to arbitrary paths, which is a major limitation for the claimed offline cinematography and world-simulation use cases.

The method is not truly model-agnostic despite broad wording. Omni Guidance depends on specific affordances of Diffusion Forcing or related noise-level conditioning, and performance is shown to depend strongly on the backbone's training distribution and context window.

The paper's theoretical framing is not fully convincing. The compositional distribution and guided-score derivation are plausible but somewhat informal, and the move from the ideal conditional formulation to the practical merged guidance term is heuristic rather than well justified.

The results lack uncertainty reporting beyond averages over 40 generations. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or robustness analysis are provided, which is problematic given stochastic video generation metrics can be noisy.

Important deployment tradeoffs remain underdeveloped, including memory cost, manual setup cost for cyclic conditioning, failure under external image conditioning, failure for wide-baseline loop closure, and inability to support online generation.

strengths: Clear and timely problem formulation: predefined camera trajectories expose a real limitation of autoregressive long video generation, namely inability to plan around future camera poses and avoid collisions.

The proposed Generative View Stitching method is technically elegant: it adapts diffusion stitching to video in a training-free way and leverages Diffusion Forcing capabilities rather than requiring a custom-trained stitching model.
Omni Guidance is a meaningful addition, with a plausible derivation and convincing ablations showing improved consistency across stochasticity settings and reduced oversmoothing tradeoffs.

The empirical section is strong overall: comparisons against autoregressive history guidance and StochSync cover diverse trajectories, loop closure, collision avoidance, frame consistency, and visual quality, with results averaged over 40 generations.
The paper includes useful ablations on loop closing, stochasticity, sampling timesteps, chunking profile, backbone variants, and inference cost, which substantially supports the main claims.
Qualitative examples, especially staircase navigation and impossible-staircase loop closure, are compelling and help demonstrate capabilities that are difficult to capture with metrics alone.

The limitations section is unusually honest and informative, clearly identifying failure cases such as online settings, external image conditioning, wide-baseline loop closure, and manually specified cyclic conditioning windows.
weaknesses: The strongest results depend on manually designed spatial/cyclic conditioning windows for each trajectory, which limits scalability to arbitrary camera paths and weakens the claim of a general-purpose camera-guided solution.

Although the method is advertised as compatible with off-the-shelf Diffusion Forcing video models, the main evaluation relies on a specific RealEstate10K-trained 8-frame model; broader validation on stronger modern video backbones or more diverse datasets would make the claim more convincing.

The evaluation uses proxy metrics such as MEt3R, VBench IQ/AQ, and depth-threshold collision detection, but lacks human preference studies or task-specific validation of perceived temporal coherence and camera fidelity.

The baselines are reasonable but not exhaustive: retrieval-augmented AR and StochSync are adapted, but comparisons to recent camera-controlled video generation, 3D-aware planning/rendering, or stronger memory-based long-video methods are limited.

The method is offline and computationally/memory intensive, with high VRAM use for long sequences; the practical tradeoff versus autoregressive methods is somewhat under-discussed for deployment settings.

Loop closure and collision avoidance are demonstrated on synthetic/chosen camera trajectories, but the robustness of the method on naturally specified user trajectories or complex real-world scene layouts remains uncertain.

Some central claims, such as generating collision-free videos and being faithful to the full trajectory, are supported empirically but not guaranteed; failures in wide-baseline and structurally ambiguous trajectories show these properties are still backbone- and trajectory-dependent.
